story.title: Windows Server 2028 public preview bets on a security-first approach - Ars Technica

facts.text: Microsoft’s Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core .
The update eliminated NVMe translation through a SCSI stack while improving speeds and reducing overhead.
Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance.
STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance.
In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations.
Secure baselines were available but not the default.
Microsoft says that concern is now managed: “The s ecure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup.
That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened. ”
Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years.
With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information.
After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.
Microsoft has unveiled a public preview of Windows Server 2028 with a new approach to security by default.
As Ars Technica reports , the system will introduce Hardened Server Core, a set of settings that, according to the company, aligns with strengthened U.S.
Department of Defense guidelines, including the DISA Security Technical Implementation Guide recommendations.
It was already added to Windows Server 2025 in an update, but administrators had to activate the feature manually at the time.
The new stack eliminates NVMe translation through SCSI and, according to Microsoft, is expected to reduce overhead and improve performance.
The release notes list a known issue with the implementation of TLS hybrid key exchange: if hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server, the LSASS service may crash.
Until the bug is fixed, Microsoft recommends disabling such key exchange groups.
The hardened settings will be available only for Server Core installations.
The company urged users to test the build and report which specific settings interfere with applications.
Microsoft will also strengthen requirements for authentication through Remote Desktop and PowerShell script block logging.
Hardware-supported security mechanisms, including Secure Boot and DMA requirements, will not be applied until a later preview build.
